subject: Effective shade values for small animals in the undergrowth (micro_ncep)

messages.author: d9c7d6ab90c62b6b
messages.subject: Effective shade values for small animals in the undergrowth (micro_ncep)
parts:
Hi all,

One of my study species is a small terrestrial frog (Crinia signifera). At my study sites, they generally spend the daytime hidden amongst dense vegetation (<0.5m height) in wetland areas that lack any canopy cover. As such, they are always out of the direct sun. In contrast at night, they can often found in more exposed positions on top of vegetation or at the edges of pools where they would be exposed to the night sky. 

My feeling was that a reasonable location to estimate their microclimate would be at approx 5cm soil depth under high shade (0.9) during the day and at a surface height of 0.01 m under lower shade (0.1 to 0.4) at night. Does this seem a reasonable plan? With regard to the daytime shade value, does it matter that the vegetation providing cover is so low? I notice the reference temperature (at 2m) reported seems to be consistent whether at 0.1 or 0.9 shade values, suggesting this isn't affected by cover height. 

Many thanks,

Tom

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Effective shade values for small animals in the undergrowth (micro_ncep)
parts:
Hi Tom,

I've got them calling in the park opposite my house.

That plan sounds sensible - I'd play around with different shade constraints and see what happens. Different ponds will have different amounts of shade, from a bare farm dam at one extreme to one surrounded by think veg at the other. You were referring to shade as fractional in your question, but it is in units of % for the model input - just checking that you're aware of this. You could set the parameter 'shdburrow' to 2, so they are always retreating in the shade and you could play with either limiting the minimum depth they can retreat to or let them go as deep as they need to avoid temperature extremes, so you can assess if they need access to deep cracks at certain times of the year.

You're correct that the reference temperature will not be affected by shade - it is simply an hourly interpolation of the weather station input data (as is the reference wind speed and humidity) - a non-microclimate variable though it can be used to estimate the temperature an animal would be exposed to if it climbed high off the ground and out of the boundary layer.

Note that if you run the soil moisture model, set the soil properties to clay, and put a multiplier on the rainfall (the 'rainmult' parameter) to account for a catchment, you can do a pretty good prediction of a wetland. Check the 'POOLDEP' output in metout to see what the estimated depth of water pooling on the surface is. This will also cause the soil to become waterlogged for more of the year, and may better capture the microclimate that C. signifera experiences by hanging around wetlands.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Effective shade values for small animals in the undergrowth (micro_ncep)
parts:
Hi Mike (and all),

Edited:

Thanks for your responses and suggestions.

I would like to also use the soil moisture model. However, the wetland sites I sampled are sphagnum peat bogs, so with organic rather than mineral soils. These I understand are likely to have low mineral content (primarily silicate), low thermal conductivity and very low bulk densities. Given this, would it be expected that the models would work just as well for these?

If so, in the context of a sphagnum peat bog, am I correct in interpreting the inputs as follows: 

Thcond = x, Soil minerals thermal conductivity (W/mK) --> thermal conductivity of silicate (presuming this to be the primary mineral)
Density = x, Soil minerals density (Mg/m3) --> the inorganic ('ash') content of the soil
SpecHeat = x, Soil minerals specific heat (J/kg-K) --> again of silicate?
BulkDensity = x, Soil bulk density (Mg/m3)  --> have lit values for sphagnum bog. 

Alternatively, I have also been able to find values for the thermal conductivity (and specific heat) of dried sphagnum moss peat soils. But i'm not sure if these could be used in place of the first three inputs?

Many thanks.

Tom

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Effective shade values for small animals in the undergrowth (micro_ncep)
parts:
Hi Tom,

Probably the thermal conditions in those peat bogs are driven by the moisture content more than anything. You can try and make the thermal properties of the soil close to peat. Note that you're specifying the solid non-water thermal components of the soil, and the overall thermal properties of the soil are then finally determined by the model from the relative amount of air, water and 'soil minerals'. There are values for organic material in Campbell and Norman 1998 Table 8.2:

Density: 1.3 Mg/m3
Spec. heat: 1920 J/kg-K
Thermal cond: 0.25 W/m-K

But you might also want to play around with the rainmult parameter to simulate a kind of catchment effect concentrating the rain if it is a little wetland - if you add deeper clay layers you can end up with quite a good simulation of a wetland.

But, as always, the main thing is to have good quality microclimatic data to compare with.

All the best,
Mike
